How an Iowa OWI Ignition Interlock Defense Attorney Can Help You Keep Driving

An ignition interlock device (IID) requirement can follow an OWI conviction in Iowa — and it can disrupt your daily life in ways you did not expect. You may need to blow into a device before your car starts. You may be subject to random retests while driving. A failed test or missed calibration can trigger new legal problems fast.

At Henkels & Baker, PC, based in Dubuque, Iowa, we help people facing IID requirements or new violations related to their OWI cases.

Iowa law requires IID installation for many OWI offenders (Iowa Code § 321J). First-time convictions, repeat offenses, and high BAC cases can all lead to this requirement. The rules around IIDs are strict. Even a small mistake — like using mouthwash before a test — can result in a reported failure. That failure can then trigger a hearing, a suspension, or worse.

An OWI defense attorney can review your case and push back on unfair IID violations. Not every reported failure is a true failure. Not every IID requirement is imposed correctly.

Henkels & Baker, PC, works to protect your rights when the system moves against you.

How Henkels & Baker Responds to Ignition Interlock Issues

At Henkels & Baker, PC, we look at the full picture — not just the device order itself, but how it connects to your larger OWI case. Our approach begins with a thorough review of the facts, the procedures used, and whether the IID requirement was imposed correctly under Iowa law.

We then review the facts that led to the IID requirement. We look at the traffic stop, the arrest, and the test results. If any part of the process was flawed, that matters.

A faulty breath test or an unlawful stop may give us grounds to challenge the underlying charge — and by extension, the interlock order tied to it.

Iowa law under Iowa Code § 321J links IID requirements directly to OWI convictions and license reinstatement. That means the outcome of your criminal case can shape whether you face an interlock requirement at all. Our defense team works to address both the criminal charge and the licensing consequences simultaneously.

We also look at how the IID requirement was imposed.

Courts and the Iowa DOT each play a role in interlock orders. If proper procedures were not followed, there may be room to push back. Our firm can review every step to find those openings.

Not every case ends with charges dropped. When full dismissal is not feasible, we work to reduce the charge or limit the scope of any interlock requirement. Our goal is to protect your license, your record, and your ability to get to work and live your life.

Your prior record, the strength of the evidence, and the county where your case is filed all shape which options are available to you.

Your Iowa OWI Ignition Interlock Case Step by Step

Iowa OWI cases move through several distinct stages. Each stage has its own deadlines, and missing one can cost you your license or limit your defense options.

Stage 1: Arrest and the 10-Day Window (Days 1–10)

After an OWI arrest in Iowa, the clock starts right away. Iowa law gives you just 10 days to request an administrative hearing with the Iowa Department of Transportation (DOT). If you miss this window, your license suspension becomes automatic.

During this stage, your job is to gather any paperwork from the arrest — your temporary license, the officer’s report, and any test results. Your attorney files the request for a hearing and begins pulling the case records for review.

Stage 2: DOT Administrative Hearing (Weeks 2–6)

This hearing is separate from your criminal case. It deals only with your driving privileges. The Iowa DOT will review whether the stop was lawful and whether the testing process followed proper procedures.

Your attorney may challenge the implied consent notice, the calibration of the breath test device, or the officer’s basis for the stop. Winning here can delay or prevent a license suspension — including any IID requirement tied to reinstatement.

Stage 3: Criminal Court Proceedings (Weeks 4–16)

Your criminal OWI charge is handled in the Iowa District Court in Dubuque, which is part of the First Judicial District. First appearances, arraignments, and pre-trial conferences happen during this phase. Your attorney reviews all evidence, files any motions to suppress, and negotiates with the prosecutor.

Under Iowa Code § 321J, a first-offense OWI conviction carries mandatory IID installation as a condition of license reinstatement. Challenging the charge early can affect whether that requirement applies at all.

Stage 4: IID Compliance or Challenge (Months 3–6)

If an IID is ordered — either by the court or the DOT — you are obligated to install a state-approved device through a certified Iowa provider before you can drive again. The device logs every startup attempt, and any violation can trigger a longer restriction period.

Your OWI defense attorney can review whether the IID order was applied correctly and whether any exemptions or modifications may apply to your case under Iowa DOT rules.

Stage 5: Case Resolution and Record (Months 4–12)

Your case ends with a plea, a dismissal, or a verdict. If you are convicted, the court sets the terms — including how long the IID stays on your vehicle. Iowa allows some first-time offenders to pursue a deferred judgment (907.3), which may keep a conviction off their permanent record if all conditions are met.

Your attorney works to get the best outcome available and helps you understand what comes next — including when and how to apply for full license reinstatement through the Iowa DOT.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Can I drive to work while the ignition interlock device is installed on my car?

Yes, you can drive your vehicle during the interlock period as long as you pass each breath test before starting it. The device does not restrict where you go — it only prevents the car from starting if alcohol is detected.

2. What happens if I miss the deadline to request a license hearing after an Iowa OWI arrest?

Iowa gives you a short window — often just 10 days — to request a hearing before an automatic suspension kicks in. If that deadline passes, your license may be suspended without any chance to contest it.

3. Will I have to pay for the ignition interlock device myself?

In most cases, yes — the cost of the device, installation, and monthly monitoring fees falls on the driver. These costs can add up over several months, so it helps to know what to expect before your case is resolved.

4. Does an ignition interlock violation count as a new OWI offense?

A violation — such as a failed breath test or a missed rolling retest — is not automatically a new OWI charge, but it can trigger a review of your interlock requirement. Iowa courts may extend your interlock period or impose other consequences based on the violation.

5. Can a passenger blow into the ignition interlock device for me?

Iowa law prohibits anyone other than the driver from providing the breath sample. Doing so may be treated as tampering with the device, which can be considered a serious misdemeanor and lead to serious legal consequences on top of your existing OWI case, such as up to 1 year in jail and fines from $430 to $2,560.
